pedagogy.summary:
• Age / Topic — 5–7; Seasons & Weather Patterns (CONCEPTUAL, 0.11): weather changes with the seasons — spring rain/new growth, warm long-day summer, cooling autumn/falling leaves, cold short-day winter — and this pattern REPEATS every year.
• Standards — UK (DfE, ANCHOR): KS1 Year 1 'Seasonal changes' (statutory): 'observe changes across the four seasons'; 'observe and describe weather associated with the seasons and how day length varies.' A core KS1 science topic. State tier: DEFERRED.
• Standards — US (NGSS): K-ESS2-1 'describe patterns over time' (VERIFIED verbatim) supplies the pattern/repetition lens; the seasonal-cause mechanism (Earth's tilt/orbit) is explicitly NOT required here (that is the later Earth's Spin & Orbit topic) — keep it observational.
• Operational details — Two ideas: (1) each season has characteristic weather AND day length; (2) the sequence is a repeating annual CYCLE. Teach it as a cycle, not a list — winter follows autumn follows summer follows spring and then round again. At this age keep it observational and local (what our trees, clothes, daylight look like each season); do NOT explain WHY seasons happen (avoid seeding the wrong 'closer to the Sun' cause — leave mechanism to age 7-9 Earth's Spin & Orbit). Prerequisite: Types of Weather (the vocabulary). Evidence: name four seasons + typical weather; state days longer in summer/shorter in winter; state the pattern repeats yearly.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (concrete/observational): the child NAMES the four seasons with typical weather for each, STATES that days are longer in summer and shorter in winter, and recognises the sequence as a pattern that REPEATS every year — described from observation, with no requirement to explain the cause.
bestPractices: Teach the seasons as a repeating CYCLE (a wheel that comes back round), not a one-way list, so 'it repeats every year' is built into the representation.
Anchor each season in observable local change — trees, clothing, daylight, activities — rather than generic storybook imagery, and note local variation (not everywhere has snowy winters).
Include DAY LENGTH explicitly (long summer days, short winter days) since it is a named evidence target and a concrete, chartable observation.
Keep it strictly observational at 5-7 and avoid cause: do NOT say 'summer is when Earth is closer to the Sun' (a classic misconception) — mechanism is deferred to the later orbit topic.
Link back to a running weather chart across the year so children SEE the pattern accumulate rather than being told it repeats.
Respect that seasons look different around the world (some places have wet/dry seasons, not four) — frame the four-season pattern as typical of our location.
keyRepresentations: A season WHEEL/cycle (spring→summer→autumn→winter→round again) — the canonical repeating-pattern rep.
Four paired panels: the same tree/scene shown across the four seasons to make change concrete.
A day-length bar that grows toward summer and shrinks toward winter.
A year-long weather/temperature chart where the seasonal rhythm becomes visible as accumulated data.
commonMisconceptions: 'Summer is hot because Earth is closer to the Sun.' — A very common cause-error; at this age simply avoid cause and keep to observation (mechanism is tilt/day-length, taught later).
Seasons are the same everywhere / everyone has snowy winters — seasonal weather varies by place; some regions have wet and dry seasons instead of four.
The four seasons happen in the same months worldwide — the Southern Hemisphere is opposite; at 5-7 just anchor locally and avoid overgeneralising.
Seasons are defined only by temperature — day length, plants, and animal behaviour are also part of the pattern.
The cycle has a 'start' — children may think it begins at winter/January; emphasise it's a continuous loop with no true beginning.

learn.summary: For ages 5–7, teach seasons and weather as a repeating annual CYCLE (spring→summer→autumn→winter→round again), anchored in observable local change: trees, clothing, daylight, activities, and weather. Hit three evidence targets — name the four seasons with typical weather, state that days are longer in summer and shorter in winter, and recognise the sequence repeats every year. Keep it strictly observational: do NOT explain WHY seasons happen (axial tilt/orbit is deferred to a later topic), and in particular avoid the 'summer is when Earth is closer to the Sun' cause-error. Observe day length by when it gets light/dark, never by looking toward the Sun. The preferred vehicle is a turnable season wheel whose coupled scene recomputes live as the child scrubs the year and loops back to spring; alternatives (paired panels, ordering/matching check, descriptive conversation, and a year-long chart) each serve distinct purposes and are preserved below.

activities.title: Turn the season wheel: watch the year come round again
feedback: When you land back on spring: 'You've come all the way round — it's spring again, just like at the start. The pattern didn't stop; it came round again. That's why we say it repeats every year.'
If a learner expects the loop to 'end' at winter: 'There's no true start or finish — the wheel keeps turning. We can begin anywhere and still come back round.'

Pointing at the day-length bar: 'Look how the bar is tallest around summer and shortest around winter — summer days are longer and winter days are shorter. We can tell by how early it gets dark, without ever looking at the Sun.'
activities.rationale: The target concept is a repeating annual cycle, and a wheel that loops lets a child experience the repetition and see each season's coupled weather, day length and scene change together. Scrubbing the year ties day length and weather to the same observation, and the loop builds 'repeats yearly' into the representation rather than asserting it. The shadow and day-length cues stay observational (ground-based, light/dark), with no causal 'why'. The live recompute and loop are offered as a concrete way to make the pattern vivid; a static picture can still teach the naming but cannot be scrubbed continuously through the loop. Efficacy of the interactive is proposed, not empirically established here.

K-ESS2-1: '[curriculum wording omitted; reference K-ESS2-1]' — supplies the pattern-over-time lens for seasonal weather.
learnerActions: Drag or turn a season wheel with your finger through the whole year.

Watch one familiar scene change in step: a bare tree pushes out blossom in spring, fills with green through the long summer days, turns gold and drops its leaves in autumn, and stands bare through the short winter days.
Watch a day-length bar swell toward summer and shrink toward winter as you turn, and notice that the tree's midday shadow on the ground is longer in winter than in summer.
Watch the little figure's clothes change from t-shirt to coat with the seasons.
Keep turning past winter until you land back in spring — the same scene you started with.
Say aloud what season comes after each one, and what happens after winter.
activities.intendedInsight: The seasons follow a fixed order that loops: after winter comes spring again. 'It repeats every year' is something you can discover by turning the wheel, not a sentence to memorise. Each season has characteristic weather AND a characteristic day length.

activities.title: Same scene, four seasons: name it and its weather
feedback: 'You named all four and matched each to its usual weather — spring rain and new growth, warm long-day summer, cooling autumn with falling leaves, cold short-day winter.'
If panels are left in a line: 'Try bending the line into a ring — because after winter we go back to spring, there's no real end.'
activities.rationale: Paired panels of one scene make seasonal change concrete and cleanly deliver naming and typical-weather-per-season. Offered as a scaffold: four fixed panels show the states but do not let the child move continuously through the loop, so arranging them in a ring is used to hint at the cycle. Suitable when a turnable model is unavailable; this is a design affordance, not a claim that panels are inferior or superior to other media for learning.
sourceClaims: DfE KS1 Year 1 'Seasonal changes' (statutory): 'observe changes across the four seasons'; 'observe and describe weather associated with the seasons and how day length varies.'
learnerActions: Look at four panels showing the SAME scene (e.g. one tree and sky) across spring, summer, autumn and winter.
Tap each panel to reveal its season name, the typical weather for that season, and a note on day length.
Arrange the four panels in a ring to show how the sequence loops back round.
Say the four season names in order and describe one typical kind of weather for each.
activities.intendedInsight: Each season has a characteristic look and typical weather; the four together form a sequence that comes back round.

activities.title: Build a year-long weather chart
feedback: If the chart shows it: 'Look how the warm marks bunch up in summer and the cold ones in winter — your own chart shows the pattern.'
'You noticed it gets dark much earlier in winter — that's the short winter days showing up in your observations.'
activities.rationale: Anchoring in a running chart lets children see the pattern accumulate from their own local observations rather than being told it repeats, and makes day length a measured observation. This directly reflects the pattern-over-time lens and keeps the work observational.
sourceClaims: K-ESS2-1: '[curriculum wording omitted; reference K-ESS2-1]' — supplies the pattern-over-time lens for seasonal weather.
learnerActions: Over the year, add a mark to a shared weather/temperature chart for the weather you observe locally.
Each season, compare your own trees, clothes and daylight to what you recorded.
Look back over the chart to spot the seasonal rhythm building up as real data.
Note when it gets dark across the year and compare summer with winter.
activities.intendedInsight: The seasonal pattern is something you can SEE accumulate in your own recorded observations, not just be told about. Day length is a concrete, chartable observation.

activities.title: Order and match check (after the hands-on work)
feedback: If a learner picks summer for shortest days: 'Think about how late it stays light in summer — summer has the LONGEST days; winter has the shortest.'
If the order is wrong after autumn: 'After autumn comes winter, then spring again — try turning the wheel in your head.'
activities.rationale: Ordering, matching and a day-length question map directly onto the evidence targets and serve as a confirmation check. As a recognition/ordering task it verifies the pattern rather than letting the child experience the loop, so it is best used after the hands-on work; recognition alone does not by itself elicit the child's own production or explanation.
learnerActions: Put the four seasons in order, and say what comes after autumn.
Match each season to its typical weather.
Answer: which season has the shortest days? Which has the longest?
activities.intendedInsight: A confirmation step, best used AFTER the hands-on wheel/chart work, to check whether naming, ordering, weather-matching and day-length targets have stuck. It checks the pattern but does not by itself make the child produce or explain the cycle.

activities.title: Talk about your own seasons
feedback: 'You described summer really well — warm, long days, outside in a t-shirt. What changes when autumn comes?'
If a child assumes everywhere has snowy winters: 'Some places don't get snow, and some have wet and dry seasons instead of four — our four-season pattern is what's typical here.'
activities.rationale: Open description can elicit and surface seasonal vocabulary and local variation. Offered as an optional complement — a pattern-recognition goal at 5–7 does not require open dialogue — so this supports vocabulary and personal connection rather than carrying the core cycle concept.
learnerActions: Tell someone your favourite season and describe the weather then.
Describe each season from your own experience — what you wear, what the trees look like, when it gets dark.
Say whether where you live has four seasons, or wet and dry seasons instead.
activities.intendedInsight: Seasons are lived and local; describing them from your own experience builds and reveals the vocabulary, and shows that seasons look different in different places.

constraints: Keep it strictly observational at 5–7: do NOT explain WHY seasons happen. In particular, never say 'summer is when Earth is closer to the Sun' — this is a classic, persistent misconception. The axial-tilt / day-length mechanism is deferred to a later Earth's Spin & Orbit topic.
Prerequisite: basic weather vocabulary (Types of Weather) so children can name typical weather per season.
Teach as a repeating CYCLE, not a one-way list; emphasise there is no true 'start' — children may wrongly think the year begins at winter/January.

Anchor locally and note variation: not everywhere has snowy winters; some regions have wet and dry seasons; the Southern Hemisphere is opposite. Frame the four-season pattern as typical of our location, and avoid overgeneralising to the whole world.
Address 'season = today's weather': a season lasts months and has TYPICAL (not guaranteed) weather; one odd day doesn't change the season.

Address 'the Sun switches off in winter': reframe short winter days as the Sun being up for fewer hours, not the Sun leaving. Never ask children to look at or toward the Sun, or to hold material toward the Sun; observe day length by when it gets light/dark, and observe shadows on the ground.
Seasons are not defined by temperature alone — day length, plants and animal behaviour are part of the pattern.

Paired panels and the ordering/matching check are, respectively, a scaffold and a post-activity recognition check: they show or test the pattern but do not let the child move continuously through the loop, and recognition does not by itself elicit the child's own production. The descriptive conversation supports vocabulary; none of these is claimed to be a uniquely necessary or superior medium.

A 3D/spatial treatment of the orbital cause is out of scope at this age; keep representations observational and local. This is a scope decision for this topic, not a general claim that 3D adds nothing to learning.
If a shadow observation is used, keep it an observation only (shadow on the ground, light/dark timing); do not explain shadow change via sun height, tilt or orbit at this age.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified this session. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Two source claims are marked unverified in the row: the DfE KS1 wording (prior-session fetch, not re-fetched) and the misconception-prevalence claim (Harvard 'A Private Universe', not fetched). Treat verbatim DfE wording and prevalence framing with caution; the NGSS K-ESS2-1 claim is marked verified in the row.

The source framed the live-recompute wheel as 'exactly what a static picture can't give' and rated 3D as adding 'no conceptual value' and a quiz as testing rather than teaching. These are catalog-fit judgements, not established efficacy findings; they have been softened to scoped affordances/limits here and should not be read as universal pedagogical laws.

The original recommendation described a 'high summer sun'/'low winter sun'; sun-elevation framing was kept out to avoid hinting at the deferred axial-tilt mechanism, but a SAFE ground-based shadow/day-length observation and the scene-change concreteness were preserved.

The two-tier assessment's diagnostic (odd cold day in summer) and its duration/typical-weather framing were preserved as misconception handling in constraints and feedback; the row's assessment fields themselves were not modified.

Independent re-audit found no critical factual or pedagogical errors; changes are scoping/preservation refinements (restored a safe shadow observation, added the post-activity scope to the check's insight) with efficacy left qualified as proposed.

probeDeeper: What season comes after summer, and after that? Does that order ever change?
Are the days longer or shorter in winter than in summer — what do you notice about when it gets dark?
If tomorrow is hot and sunny again, does that mean the season changed back? Why not?
assess.correctAnswer: No — it's still summer. One cold, rainy day doesn't change the season. Summer is a time of year that lasts for months, and the seasons follow a fixed order that repeats every year (spring, summer, autumn, winter). A single day's weather can be different from the season's usual weather.

errorPatterns.pattern: Season = today's weather — 'it's cold, so it must be winter'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Stress duration and pattern: a season lasts months and has TYPICAL weather; one odd day doesn't move the calendar. Track a week to show the season holds.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes, it's winter now, because winter is when it's cold.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Switches the season to match a single day's weather

errorPatterns.pattern: Seasons don't have a fixed repeating order — 'we might skip one'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rehearse the repeating loop with a season wheel: after summer always comes autumn, then winter, then spring, every year.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Can't state the fixed cycle or thinks seasons come in a changeable order

errorPatterns.pattern: The Sun switches off in winter — 'winter days are dark because the Sun goes away'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reframe as day length: in winter the Sun is up for fewer hours, so it gets dark earlier; the Sun doesn't switch off.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Attributes short winter days to the Sun stopping or leaving rather than being up for less time

responseLevels.gap: Says a cold day means it's winter; treats the season as whatever today's weather is.
responseLevels.full: Says it's still summer because a season is a long repeating period defined by its typical (not guaranteed) weather, names the fixed cycle, links summer/winter to longer/shorter days, and handles a new odd-day case.
responseLevels.partial: Says it's still summer and can name the seasons, but can't explain that a season lasts months with only typical weather, or muddles day length.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: It's the middle of summer, but today turned out cold and rainy. A child says, 'It must be winter now, because it's cold.' Are they right? Tell me what season it is and why.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands seasons as long, ordered, repeating periods says it's still summer despite the cold. A child who equates the season with today's weather says it's now winter — the tell — which also seeds the later weather-vs-climate distinction.
